units.title: Paper 1: Thematic study and historic environment

topics.title: Option 10: Crime and punishment in Britain, c1000-present

subtopics.title: The process of change in crime and punishment

outcomes.text: Explain how crime and punishment changed with British society, using patterns, turning points and the factors of attitudes, Church and government, and science and technology.
Describe medieval crimes against person, property and authority, including poaching as social crime.
Explain how the Norman Conquest and William I's Forest Laws changed definitions of crime.
Describe medieval law enforcement: tithings, hue and cry and the parish constable.
Explain the emphasis on deterrence and retribution, fines, corporal and capital punishment, and the Saxon Wergild.
Explain the Church's influence: sanctuary, benefit of clergy and trial by ordeal and why it ended.
Describe continuity and change in crimes including heresy and treason.
Explain new sixteenth-century crimes: vagabondage and witchcraft.
Describe law enforcement by town watchmen and the continued use of harsh punishments.
Explain the start of transportation and the Bloody Code.
Explain the Gunpowder Plotters' crimes and punishment in 1605.
Explain why Matthew Hopkins's witch-hunts of 1645-47 were so intense and how convicts were punished.

subtopics.title: Crime and punishment in the 18th and 19th centuries

outcomes.text: Describe highway robbery, poaching and smuggling and continuity in crime.
Explain changing definitions of crime: end of witchcraft prosecutions and the Tolpuddle Martyrs.
Describe the Fielding brothers, the growth of police forces and the start of CID.
Explain changing views on punishment: end of transportation and public execution, and the Bloody Code.
Explain prison reform and the influence of John Howard and Elizabeth Fry.
Evaluate Pentonville prison and the separate system.
Explain Robert Peel's contribution to penal reform and the Metropolitan Police.

subtopics.title: Crime and punishment in modern Britain

outcomes.text: Describe continuity and change in crime, including new forms of theft and smuggling.
Explain new definitions of crime: driving, race and drug crimes.
Describe modern policing: Neighbourhood Watch, specialisation, technology and prevention.
Explain the abolition of the death penalty and changes to prisons, open prisons and youth treatment.
Describe non-custodial alternatives to prison.
Explain the treatment of Conscientious Objectors in both World Wars.
Explain the Derek Bentley case and its significance for abolishing the death penalty.

topics.title: Option 10 historic environment: Whitechapel, c1870-c1900

outcomes.text: Describe Whitechapel's housing, overcrowding, the Peabody Estate and workhouses, and links between environment and crime.
Describe Whitechapel's inhabitants: poverty, lodging houses, pubs and migration from Ireland and Eastern Europe.
Explain the role of the beat constable and H division and the difficulties of policing slums.
Describe policing problems: alcohol, prostitution, protection rackets, gangs, demonstrations and attacks on Jewish people.
Describe detective techniques of sketches, photographs and interviews and the problems of police cooperation.
Explain the Jack the Ripper investigation, media reporting and the Whitechapel Vigilance Committee.
Describe the Metropolitan Police, recruits, CID, the Home Secretary, Sir Charles Warren and public attitudes.
Know local and national sources for Whitechapel such as census, Booth's survey, police records, Old Bailey records and Punch cartoons.
Judge the strengths and weaknesses of sources and frame historical enquiries.

topics.title: Option 11: Medicine in Britain, c1250-present

subtopics.title: The process of change in medicine

outcomes.text: Explain how medicine changed with British society, using patterns, turning points and the factors of individuals and institutions, science and technology, and attitudes.
Explain supernatural and religious explanations of disease.
Explain rational explanations: four humours, miasma and Galen's influence.
Describe medieval prevention and treatment: religious actions, bloodletting, purging and purifying the air.
Describe medical training and care: physicians, apothecaries, barber surgeons, hospitals and herbal remedies.
Explain how the Black Death of 1348-49 was treated and how people tried to stop its spread.
Explain continuity and change in ideas on disease, Sydenham's diagnosis, the printing press and the Royal Society.
Describe changes in prevention, treatment and care in the community and hospitals.
Explain improvements in training and the influence of Vesalius.
Explain William Harvey's discovery of the circulation of the blood.
Explain how the Great Plague of 1665 was treated and how people tried to stop its spread.
Explain the influence of Pasteur's Germ Theory and Koch's work on microbes.
Describe improvements in hospital care and Nightingale's influence on nursing.
Explain the impact of anaesthetics and antiseptics on surgery.
Describe vaccination and the Public Health Act of 1875.
Explain Jenner and the development of vaccination.
Explain the 1854 London cholera outbreak, John Snow and the Broad Street pump.
Explain how genetic and lifestyle factors advanced understanding of illness.
Explain improved diagnosis through blood tests, scans and monitors.
Explain the impact of the NHS, magic bullets, antibiotics and high-tech treatment.
Describe mass vaccination and government lifestyle campaigns.
Explain the development of penicillin by Fleming, Florey and Chain.
Explain the twenty-first-century fight against lung cancer, including diagnosis, treatment and government action.

topics.title: Option 11 historic environment: Western Front, 1914-18

outcomes.text: Describe the Western Front's terrain, trench system and effect on medical treatment.
Describe conditions needing treatment: trench ill health, wounds from rifles and explosives, shrapnel, infection, head injuries and gas.
Describe the RAMC, nurses, stretcher bearers, ambulances and the stages of the chain of evacuation.
Explain new surgical and medical techniques: the Thomas splint, mobile x-rays and the Cambrai blood bank.
Explain early twentieth-century medicine: aseptic surgery, x-rays and blood transfusion and storage.

subtopics.title: Using sources on the Western Front

outcomes.text: Know national and local sources such as army records, newspapers, personal accounts and hospital records.
Judge the strengths and weaknesses of sources and frame historical enquiries.

topics.title: Option 12: Warfare and British society, c1250-present

subtopics.title: The process of change in warfare

Explain the effect of the longbow, schiltrons, gunpowder and cannon and the decline of the knight.
Describe recruitment and training in the feudal army.
Explain the impact of feudal duties and plunder on civilians.
Explain why the Battle of Falkirk (1298) ended as it did, including Wallace and Edward I.
Explain why the Battle of Agincourt (1415) ended as it did, including Henry V.
Describe the army's changing makeup: musketeers, pikemen, dragoons, cavalry and the standing army.
Explain the impact of new muskets and pistols.
Describe recruitment and training, including the New Model Army.
Explain the effect of recruitment and requisitioning on civilians.
Explain why the Battle of Naseby (1645) ended as it did, including Cromwell.
Describe the decline of the cavalry and changes in the army's composition.
Explain the effect of rifles, field guns, artillery, steam transport and mass production of weapons.
Explain Cardwell's army reforms and professionalisation.
Explain how newspapers and photography changed attitudes in the Crimean and Boer Wars.
Explain why the Battle of Waterloo (1815) ended as it did, including Wellington.
Explain why the Battle of Balaclava (1854) ended as it did, including Lord Raglan.
Describe the growth of logistics corps and bomb disposal units.
Explain the impact of machine guns, tanks, chemical and nuclear weapons, radar, aircraft and high-tech warfare, and guerrilla warfare.
Describe conscription, national service, recruitment of women and a professional army.
Explain the Home Front, fear of nuclear war and attitudes to Conscientious Objectors.
Explain how war reporting, censorship and propaganda affected attitudes.
Explain trench warfare, attrition, the Somme outcome and General Haig's role.
Explain the outcome of the Iraq War (2003) and its use of high-tech weapons and surveillance.

topics.title: Option 12 historic environment: London and the Second World War

outcomes.text: Explain London's role as capital, port and industrial centre and target for bombers.
Describe preparations: evacuation, Anderson shelters and gas masks.
Describe attacks on the East End docks, Black Saturday and the V2 attack on Deptford, and the bombs used.
Explain the Blitz's impact: air-raid precautions, Tube shelters, the South Hallsville and Bethnal Green disasters, leisure and morale.
Describe London's response: the Royal Family, the Cabinet War Rooms and Dig for Victory.
Explain the purpose of the Blitz and government propaganda and censorship.
Know local and national sources such as personal accounts, Mass Observation, newsreels and memoirs.
Judge the strengths and weaknesses of sources and frame historical enquiries.

topics.title: Option 13: Migrants in Britain, c800-present

Describe the city of York under the Vikings.
Explain change and continuity in reasons for migration, including migrants from Europe and Africa.

Describe migrants' relations with authorities and locals and their impact on culture, trade, industry and farming.
Explain the experience of Flemish and Walloon migrants in Sandwich and Canterbury.
Explain the experience of Huguenots in seventeenth-century England.
Explain reasons for migration from Ireland, Europe and the Empire.
Describe the context: Industrial Revolution, urbanisation, transatlantic slavery, the Empire and civil liberties.
Describe migrants' relations with authorities and locals and the role of the media.
Explain migrants' impact on culture, trade, industry, politics and cities.
Explain Liverpool's role in migration and the experience of Irish migrants.
Explain the experience of Jewish migrants in the late nineteenth-century East End.
Explain reasons for migration from Ireland, Europe, the Empire and Commonwealth, including refugees and asylum seekers.

Describe anti-immigration and equal rights movements, the Race Relations Act 1965 and the media.
Explain migrants' impact on culture, politics, cities, public services and the economy.
Explain migrants' experiences in mid-twentieth-century Bristol.
Explain the experience of Asian migrants in Leicester from 1945.

topics.title: Option 13 historic environment: Notting Hill, c1948-c1970

subtopics.title: Housing and Caribbean culture in Notting Hill

outcomes.text: Explain Caribbean migration to Notting Hill and its housing problems, Rachman, Bruce Kenrick and Portobello Road market.
Describe Caribbean influence on shops, cafes, shebeens, clubs, All Saints Road and self-help 'pardner' schemes.
Explain racism and policing: the 1958 riots, Kelso Cochrane's murder and Mosley's Union Movement.
Describe Black activism: Claudia Jones, the 1959 Carnival, Frank Crichlow, the Mangrove, Black Panthers and the Mangrove Nine.
Describe post-war Britain: reconstruction, labour demand, the Commonwealth, the Swinging Sixties, poverty and policing.
Know local and national sources such as community publications, council and police records, memoirs, opinion polls and television reports.
Judge the strengths and weaknesses of sources and frame historical enquiries.
